title: The Wage You Don't Pay Yourself Is Quietly Inflating Your Profit Number
linkedin:
Every owner-led P&L has a profit line. Not every owner-led P&L has an honest one.

Here's a pattern we see across owner-led SMEs. The owner draws far less than the market rate for the role they're actually doing, often three jobs compressed into one modest wage. The business books that gap as profit, because there's nowhere else for it to sit. The margin looks stronger every year, partly because the discount underneath it keeps compounding.

The problem isn't the accounting. It's what gets built on top of that number.

A pricing review benchmarked against a discounted owner wage lands on a price that only works while the owner keeps discounting themselves. A hiring case for a second salesperson can look stronger than it actually is once you account for what happens to margin the day someone has to be paid properly to do part of what the owner currently absorbs for free. A second site, modelled off the existing P&L, assumes the owner can absorb the same unpaid load twice over. They can't.

The fix is a straightforward exercise, even if it's an uncomfortable one the first time. Price your own role at what it would genuinely cost to hire a replacement, add that as a real wage line, then see what profit is left. For some businesses the number barely moves. For others, a business that looked healthy is closer to break even.

Either way, it's a truer number to plan around.

Honest question for the business owners in the group: when did you last price your own role at what it would actually cost to replace you?

Most owner-led P&Ls look healthy partly because the owner is paid well under market rate for everything they actually do. That gap gets booked as profit, because there's nowhere else for it to sit. Which is fine, until that number becomes the basis for a pricing decision, a new hire, or a second site, all of which quietly assume the discount will keep going forever.

Worth doing the exercise properly at least once a year, even if the answer stings a bit.

A pattern worth checking in your own numbers. That gap gets counted as profit because there is nowhere else in the accounts for it to sit. Over a few years it becomes invisible, and the margin looks stronger with every passing year mostly because the discount underneath it keeps growing.

The issue is not the accounting itself. It is what gets built on top of that understated number. A pricing decision, a new hire, or a second location, all modelled off a P&L that assumes the owner will keep working at a discount indefinitely, can look far more affordable on paper than they actually are.
